interview_parallel: Razorpay / Postman early-career SWE round — code review: catch subtle bugs an AI pair might introduce in a simple filter utility
acceptance_criteria: Function returns only users whose age is strictly greater than 18 (not >= 18)
Function excludes users where age is undefined, null, or not a finite number
Function does not mutate the input array
Function returns an empty array when the input is empty or all users are excluded

seeded_mistakes.bug_description: Off-by-one in age comparison: uses `>= 18` instead of `> 18`. A user who is exactly 18 is NOT 'over 18' — they should be excluded, but this code includes them.
seeded_mistakes.why_compass_might_suggest_it: LLMs frequently confuse 'over 18' (strictly greater) with 'at least 18' (greater-or-equal). The phrase 'adult' or 'over 18' in natural language is ambiguous; the model defaults to the more common >= pattern used in age-gate forms that say '18 or older'.
detection_signals: Unit test: filterAdults([{ name: 'Alex', age: 18 }]) should return [] — the buggy code returns [{ name: 'Alex', age: 18 }]
Code review: scanning for >= in a filter that was specified as 'over N'

seeded_mistakes.bug_description: Missing guard for absent `age` field: when `user.age` is `undefined`, the expression `undefined >= 18` evaluates to `false` in JavaScript, which accidentally produces the correct exclusion result — BUT if `user.age` is `NaN` (e.g., parsed from a malformed string upstream), `NaN >= 18` also returns `false`, masking the bug. More critically, the spec says missing-age users must be explicitly excluded; relying on implicit NaN coercion is fragile and not intent-revealing.
seeded_mistakes.why_compass_might_suggest_it: JavaScript's implicit type coercion means `undefined >= 18` returns false without a type error, so the LLM's test suite (if it has one) passes on undefined inputs. The LLM does not add a guard because the comparison 'already works' for undefined. This is a classic case of accidentally-correct code that breaks with a different upstream type.
detection_signals: Unit test: filterAdults([{ name: 'Bob' }]) returns [] — this passes with the buggy code, masking the missing explicit guard
Unit test: filterAdults([{ name: 'Carol', age: NaN }]) should return [] — the buggy code also returns [] here, but for the wrong reason
Code review: no typeof or Number.isFinite guard present in the filter callback

rubric_anchors.check: Learner identifies the >= vs > off-by-one and names the exact line where it appears
Learner identifies the missing explicit guard for undefined/non-numeric age, even if the accidental coercion behaviour happens to return the right result for undefined
Learner explains WHY the LLM made each mistake (ambiguous natural-language spec, implicit JS coercion) rather than just stating 'it is wrong'
Corrected code is clean, intent-revealing, and passes all four acceptance criteria — no new bugs introduced in the fix

common_verification_traps: Accepts the code as correct because undefined >= 18 happens to return false in JavaScript — the missing guard is invisible if you only test the happy path and the undefined path
Misses the >= vs > distinction because they mentally read 'adults' as meaning >= 18, matching the LLM's interpretation rather than the spec
Writes a corrected version that handles undefined but still uses >= 18, fixing only one of the two bugs
